entities.name: Jehuda Cresques
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jehudà Cresques, also known as Jaume Riba after his conversion, was a pivotal figure in European cartography during the late 14th and early 15th centuries, inheriting and extending the renowned Majorcan cartographic tradition. Born into the prominent Jewish Cresques family of Palma, Majorca, he was the son of the master cartographer Abraham Cresques, with whom he is believed to have co-authored the seminal Catalan Atlas of 1375. His work represents a crucial nexus where the advanced practical navigation of the Majorcan school met the burgeoning ambitions of Iberian maritime powers, particularly Portugal, at the dawn of the Age of Discovery.

Following the violent anti-Jewish pogroms of 1391 in Majorca, Jehudà Cresques converted to Christianity, adopting the name Jaume Riba. This forced conversion, while a personal tragedy, paradoxically positioned him to play an even more significant role in the transmission of cartographic knowledge. His expertise in crafting highly accurate portolan charts and world maps, which combined empirical data from mariners with advanced geometric projections, made him highly sought after. Prince Henry the Navigator, the architect of Portugal's maritime expansion, actively recruited Cresques, reportedly offering a substantial sum to bring him to Sagres around 1410 to head a newly established navigational school. This move was instrumental in transferring the sophisticated Majorcan techniques directly to the nascent Portuguese cartographic and navigational efforts.
